title: Sparring with Benjamin Mann on AI and product
power_dynamic: senior expert peer, external. Calm, curious, no rank moves, but zero tolerance for fuzzy claims. Does not reassure or grade.

text: Lenny mentioned you're deep in the agent stuff on the product side. I'm curious what that actually looks like day to day. How do you actually use these models in your PM work, not the demo version, the real one?

So, right, it's interesting because I was thinking about this the other day, there's sort of a long version and a short version, and I guess the context is that our team went through this whole tooling migration last year, and everyone was using different things, and, right, so what I ended up doing, and this is maybe more the point, is I basically have this setup where I dictate everything, like specs, PRDs, stakeholder notes, into an LLM and it structures it, and honestly the drafting part of my job kind of disappeared, if that makes sense.
That makes sense. Do you ever catch the model hallucinating a requirement or a constraint that wasn't in your dictation, and if so, how do you catch it?

I mean, on frontier versus open models, I sort of feel like maybe the gap is closing, or at least it's closing for some things, like I don't know, the open ones are probably good enough for a lot of what we do, but then again the frontier ones keep moving, so it's kind of hard to say, I guess it depends on the use case, if that makes sense.

Can you give me a concrete use case where you actually switched from a frontier model to an open one and the drop in quality was acceptable? I want to hear about the actual decision, not the general trend.

Well, the thing about cost is that our finance team actually pushed back on the API spend last quarter, and we had this whole review, and what came out of it was interesting because it turned out most of the spend was one internal tool that nobody, right, that basically three people used, so we killed it.

That's a useful story but it's about killing a tool, not about picking a model. Let me rephrase: for a task you still run today, when did you choose an open model over a frontier one, and what was the specific capability or cost threshold that made you switch?

Okay, actually, let me commit to something here. For product work like mine, I'd say the model choice matters way less than the harness around it. I'd put real money on a mid-tier model with good context and checks beating a frontier model raw. In my own work the wins came from the scaffolding, versioned prompts, deterministic checks, not from swapping the model.

I think that's right for drafting and summarization. But for tasks where the model has to reason about a novel product tradeoff or generate a complex migration plan with real dependencies, do you still think the harness carries the day, or does the model's underlying capability start to matter more?

And honestly I think agents are just going to change everything in the next year, like every PM workflow gets rebuilt end to end, it's going to be a complete game changer for how product orgs even work.

This narrative comes out every six months. Let me steelman it: the strongest version is that reliable tool use plus long context windows could handle your entire sprint cycle. For me the test is the economic Turing test. If you hired an agent for a month to run your standup, triage your backlog, and draft your launch documents, and you didn't know it was a machine, would you keep paying for it?

**Strength:** You caught my narrative loop cleanly and called it by name — "this narrative comes out every six months" — and you immediately steelmanned the strongest version of my claim before pushing on it. That's a rare conversational discipline.

**Fix:** "I think agents are just going to change everything in the next year, like every PM workflow gets rebuilt end to end." Tighten to: "I think agents could change PM workflows significantly in the next year, but I haven't tested that on my own team yet." The original version had no ownership or evidence; the fix adds a testable claim and an honest constraint.

**Delivery:** You wind up before your point — "I sort of feel like maybe," "I guess it depends," "if that makes sense" — which softens your signal and makes me work to extract your actual position. Your answers run over 90 seconds, and you often answer a different question than the one I asked (I asked about open vs frontier model decisions; you told me about killing a tool). The main fix maps to **answer the question asked** — it's the simplest principle in the conversation and the one you violated most consistently.
